experiences.name: Guelaguetza (The Offering)
experiences.dateDetails: July; principal celebrations traditionally on two Mondays
experiences.why: Regional dances, woven and embroidered costumes and community traditions from across Oaxaca.
experiences.artPairing: Museo Textil de Oaxaca; Zapotec rug makers, black pottery and carved alebrijes.
experiences.landscapePairing: Sierra Norte cloud forests, mountains and mineral terraces at Hierve el Agua.
experiences.tagline: Delegations from Oaxaca's eight regions dance on a hillside amphitheater, then share gifts
experiences.story:
Guelaguetza is a Zapotec word for reciprocal giving, and in July Oaxaca City holds its biggest celebration under that name. On two Mondays in late July, delegations from the state's regions perform their dances in an open-air amphitheater on the Cerro del Fortín, overlooking the city. At the end of each dance they throw gifts into the audience: fruit, bread, small baskets, even pineapples. City parades, food and mezcal fairs and concerts fill the weeks around it.

The Flor de Piña dancers from the Papaloapan region carry pineapples on their shoulders; the Danza de la Pluma features huge feathered headdresses. The colors are those of handwoven huipiles and embroidered skirts, and the music is brass and marimba. The amphitheater is steep and seating is tiered, with paid sections in front and free sections at the top. Plan ahead: rows of steps are the main access challenge.
experiences.wonderMoment: When the Flor de Piña dancers finish and pineapples start flying up into the stands.

experiences.tagline: Glowing paper warriors the size of houses, pushed through the night by chanting dancers
experiences.story:
Every August 2 to 7, Aomori city in northern Honshu parades its nebuta: enormous lantern floats of samurai, gods and demons made from washi paper over wire frames and lit from inside. Each is about nine metres wide and five tall, painted in strong reds, blues and blacks, and takes a master nebuta-shi most of a year to design and build. About twenty of them roll through the streets each night.

It is a festival to join, not only watch. Thousands of haneto dancers in flower hats and bells hop alongside the floats, shouting 'Rassera! Rassera!', while taiko drums, flutes and cymbals fill the street. Each float is turned and pushed toward the crowd so the glowing faces seem to lunge at you. Visitors can rent a haneto costume and dance. On the final night the winning floats are carried on boats across Aomori Bay under fireworks.
experiences.wonderMoment: A glowing paper warlord twice your height swings toward you out of the dark, eyes blazing, while hundreds of dancers bounce around it shouting 'Rassera!'

experiences.story:
The Kumbh Mela rotates between four river cities, and Nashik with nearby Trimbakeshwar hosts the Simhastha, held when Jupiter is in Leo, once every twelve years. Legend says a drop of the nectar of immortality fell here. The year is long, but its peaks are the Amrit Snan (royal bath) days, when the akharas, the orders of Hindu ascetics, process to the river in strict order to bathe before anyone else; Shaiva orders bathe at Kushavarta tank in Trimbakeshwar and Vaishnava orders at Ramkund in Nashik.

Before dawn the roads fill with chanting, conches and drums. Gurus ride on decorated chariots and elephants under umbrellas; ranks of Naga sadhus, naked and smeared with ash, run toward the water waving tridents and swords, plunging in with a roar. Monsoon rain often falls on top of it all. Afterwards millions of pilgrims follow, and the ghats become a sea of wet saris, marigolds and smoke from fire rituals.
experiences.wonderMoment: Just after dawn on an Amrit Snan day, the first rank of ash-covered Naga sadhus breaks into a run and plunges into the sacred tank, roaring.

experiences.story:
The Kanto Matsuri in Akita, held August 3 to 6, began as a summer ritual to ward off illness and pray for a good rice harvest. Its kanto are tall bamboo poles with crossbars carrying dozens of paper lanterns, arranged to look like ears of rice. The largest are about 12 metres tall, carry 46 lit lanterns and weigh about 50 kilograms.

After dusk, Kanto Odori avenue is closed to traffic and more than 200 poles go up at once, a forest of soft orange light along the boulevard. Performers pass each pole from hand to palm, then to the forehead, shoulder and lower back, adding extensions until it bends overhead. Flutes and drums play and the crowd shouts 'Dokkoisho!' to cheer them on. When a pole sways too far it is caught by teammates, sometimes just before it drops into the audience.

experiences.story:
The Tattoo began in 1950 on the esplanade in front of Edinburgh Castle, and has run every August since, except during the pandemic. The name comes from the old military call for soldiers to return to their quarters at night. Each show mixes Scottish pipe bands, military bands, dancers and invited performers from around the world, and around 220,000 people see it every summer.

The show starts after dark, with the castle lit behind the arena and projections playing across its stone walls. Snare drums crack and echo off the walls, and the crowd goes quiet when the massed pipes and drums march out through the castle gatehouse, kilts swinging, a wall of sound filling the esplanade. The night air is often cool and damp, and at the end a lone piper plays from the battlements before fireworks burst over the old town.

experiences.tagline: Robed elephants, fire dancers and the Buddha's tooth relic through Kandy at night
experiences.story:
The Esala Perahera honours the Sacred Tooth Relic of the Buddha, kept in Kandy's Temple of the Tooth, and merges older processions for the island's four guardian gods. It runs for about ten nights in July or August, growing larger each night: the quieter Kumbal Perahera first, then the Randoli Perahera, named for the palanquins of the queens, ending on the full moon with a final daytime procession.

It begins with whip-crackers snapping the air to clear the road, then flag bearers, torch carriers swinging coconut-husk fires, and lines of Kandyan dancers in silver breastplates, jumping and spinning to drums. Between them walk elephants draped in embroidered cloth strung with lights. The high point is the Maligawa tusker, the temple's chief elephant, carrying the golden casket under a canopy while the crowds packed along the streets fall silent or cry out 'Sadhu'. The smell is smoke, jasmine and camphor; the noise is drums.
experiences.wonderMoment: The street goes quiet as the Maligawa tusker, glittering with lights, walks past carrying the relic casket under its canopy.

experiences.story:
Awa Odori in Tokushima, on the island of Shikoku, is Japan's largest Bon dance festival, held August 12 to 15 during Obon, when families welcome back the spirits of ancestors. Its roots go back about 400 years. Groups called ren dance through the city in tight blocks: women in straw hats folded like half-moons stepping on wooden clogs, men in a lower crouching style, all to shamisen, flutes, drums and bells. The song goes 'the dancers are fools and the watchers are fools, so you might as well dance'.

At night the city is warm and humid and full of sound. Paid grandstands line the main dance areas, so visitors can sit while ren after ren comes through, and on the side streets anyone can join a dance. A short ferry ride away across the Inland Sea, Naoshima and Teshima give the trip a calm second half: Tadao Ando's underground Chichu Art Museum, Yayoi Kusama's pumpkins on the pier and Teshima Art Museum's single drop-shaped shell.
experiences.wonderMoment: A ren of women in half-moon straw hats glides past on tiptoe in perfect unison, hands raised, while the drums speed up and the crowd starts clapping.

experiences.story:
Rhein in Flammen is a chain of summer nights on the Rhine where towns light up their riverbanks, castles and churches and set off fireworks from the water. Today there are five editions, from Bonn in May to St. Goar and Oberwesel in September. The biggest is Spay to Koblenz in August, part of Koblenz's summer festival.

As it gets dark, around 70 passenger ships form a convoy and drift north through the gorge, their decks strung with lights. At each town they pass, red Bengal flares light up the riverbank and the castles: Marksburg above Braubach, then Lahneck and Stolzenfels. Fireworks go up one after another along the route, and the sound echoes off the vineyard slopes. In Koblenz the crowds pack the promenades and the Deutsches Eck, where the Moselle joins the Rhine. The finale is a big fireworks display over Fortress Ehrenbreitstein, now paired with a drone show, reflected in black water full of ships.
experiences.wonderMoment: When the whole convoy of glowing ships lies still below Ehrenbreitstein and the fortress cliff disappears behind the finale's fireworks.

experiences.tagline: One hour, a hundred-odd tonnes of tomatoes and a town street that runs red
experiences.story:
La Tomatina began in Buñol in 1945, when a scuffle among young people at a parade turned into a tomato fight. The town banned it, then gave in, and since the 1950s it has run every last Wednesday of August. The morning starts with the palo jabón (greased pole): someone has to climb a soaped pole and grab the ham at the top. Then a water cannon signals the start and trucks roll down the narrow Calle del Cristo, tipping tomatoes onto the crowd.

For an hour it is pure chaos. The air smells sharp and sweet, the pulp is warm and ankle-deep, and the noise is laughter, shrieks and the rumble of the next truck. Rules say squash each tomato before throwing it, and stop when the second cannon fires. Afterward, locals hose down the streets and people rinse off in the river, and the acid leaves the paving stones scrubbed oddly clean.
experiences.wonderMoment: When the first truck turns into Calle del Cristo and the whole street goes red in seconds.

experiences.story:
Burning Man began in 1986 when a few friends burned a wooden figure on San Francisco's Baker Beach. It moved to Nevada's Black Rock Desert in 1990 and grew into Black Rock City, a temporary town of tens of thousands laid out in a giant arc around the Man. Nothing is sold except ice and coffee; people bring everything, give freely and leave no trace.

The playa is flat, white and endless, and in a dust storm it disappears completely. At night it turns into a field of light: art cars shaped like ships and creatures drift past blasting music, flame effects roar, and huge sculptures glow kilometers out in the open desert. On Saturday the Man burns with fireworks and a roaring crowd. On Sunday the Temple, filled all week with handwritten notes and photos of the dead, burns while tens of thousands watch in near silence.

experiences.tagline: Feathered mas bands, steel pans and towering sound systems in west London
experiences.story:
Notting Hill Carnival grew out of the Caribbean community in post-war London. Trinidad-born activist Claudia Jones organized an indoor Caribbean carnival in 1959 after the 1958 race riots, and a street fair started by Rhaune Laslett in 1966 became the carnival on the streets. It now draws around a million people across the August bank-holiday weekend.

The parade follows a loop through Notting Hill and Ladbroke Grove. Mas bands, hundreds of dancers in matching costumes of feathers, beads and sequins, move to soca from trucks, while steel bands play on rolling frames. Off the route, more than 30 sound systems stack speakers along side streets and play reggae, dub, dancehall and jungle loud enough to feel in your chest. Smoke from jerk-chicken drums fills the air, and the whole neighborhood smells of allspice and grilled corn. Sunday is the family day with the children's parade; Monday is the main event.

experiences.tagline: Bilbao's nine-day street party, opened by a rocket and a giant grinning matriarch
experiences.story:
Aste Nagusia, Bilbao's Great Week, has been the city's August fiesta in its modern form since 1978, when neighbourhood groups called konpartsak took control of the party after the Franco years. It opens on the first Saturday after 15 August with the txupinazo, a rocket fired from the Arriaga theatre balcony, and the appearance of Marijaia, a huge raised-arm figure who becomes the week's mascot.

For nine days the riverside fills with konpartsa huts serving drinks and food, while the old town hosts giants and big-heads parades, Basque rural sports, bertsolari improvised verse, open-air concerts and a fireworks contest over the Nervión each night. It is loud, informal and truly local. At the end, Marijaia is burned beside the river, and the crowd sings farewell to the summer. Most of it is free, and the city feels like one long open-air living room for a week.
experiences.wonderMoment: At the last fireworks of the week, Marijaia goes up in flames on the riverbank and thousands of people sing her goodbye.

experiences.story:
The Ducasse of Ath, in Wallonia, centres on the fourth weekend of August. Its procession of giants goes back to the 15th century and is listed by UNESCO. On Saturday afternoon Goliath and his bride are married in the church of Saint-Julien, then Goliath meets the young David in the square in front of the town hall. They trade verses, David fires his sling, and Goliath falls.

Sunday brings the full cortège: the four-metre giants Ambiorix, Mam'zelle Victoire, Samson and the two Tirants, plus the huge Cheval Bayard carrying the four Aymon brothers on its back. Bearers hidden inside make the figures spin and dance to brass bands. The crowd is dense and devoted; townspeople have carried these giants for generations. The Bayard horse dance, heavy and graceful, is the moment people wait for.
experiences.wonderMoment: The enormous Cheval Bayard, with four boys riding on its back, turns slowly in the packed street and then breaks into its dance.

experiences.story:
Charleville-Mézieres in the French Ardennes has hosted the Festival Mondial des Théâtres de Marionnettes since 1961. The town is also home to France's national puppetry school, and during the festival it becomes a meeting place for companies from dozens of countries. Programmes range from tiny tabletop shows for twenty people to large shadow plays, marionettes and object theatre in proper halls.

Much of the magic happens outdoors and free. Around the arcaded Place Ducale and the streets nearby, wandering performers, giant figures, buskers and little booths pop up all day. The pace is unhurried: you can see a dozen short shows in an afternoon, eat in a café between them, then queue for a ticketed evening piece. Above the old town, a mechanical clock with a puppet figure performs the story of the Four Aymon Sons on the hour.
experiences.wonderMoment: A giant puppet glides into the Place Ducale at dusk while the arcades fill with hundreds of people falling quiet at once.

experiences.dateDetails: Sep 18 – Oct 3, 2027 (192nd Oktoberfest), per the City of Munich's official site. The mayor taps the first keg at noon on opening Saturday in the Schottenhamel tent; the Costume and Riflemen's Parade is on the first Sunday (Sep 19).

experiences.story:
Oktoberfest began in 1810 as horse races to celebrate the wedding of Bavaria's Crown Prince Ludwig and Princess Therese, and the meadow still carries her name. Today it fills 16 days with more than a dozen big beer tents, smaller family tents and a huge funfair. It opens at noon on the first Saturday when the mayor drives a tap into the first keg and calls out "O'zapft is!" (It's tapped!). The next morning the Costume and Riflemen's Parade sends thousands of marchers, bands, horses and decorated brewery wagons through the city.

Inside the tents the sound is overwhelming: oompah bands on central stages, thousands of people standing on benches to sing, servers carrying ten mugs at a time. The air smells of roast chicken, pretzels and sugared almonds. After dark the Ferris wheel and rides throw colored light across the meadow, under the bronze Bavaria statue.
experiences.wonderMoment: At noon on opening Saturday the mayor hits the keg, the 12 cannon shots go off, and the whole tent rises roaring with the first mugs.

experiences.tagline: Giant animals of rice straw towering over a lakeside park in Niigata's rice country
experiences.story:
Niigata is one of Japan's main rice regions, and after each harvest there is a lot of straw left over. Since 2008 the Wara Art Festival at Uwasekigata Park in Niigata's Nishikan ward has turned it into art, working with students from Musashino Art University in Tokyo. They design huge figures of animals and creatures, often a T. rex, gorillas, eagles, crabs, Gajira or a samurai, and build them with local farmers over wooden frames.

The sculptures stand several metres high on the grass beside a shallow lake, with Mount Kakuda behind. They are shaggy and golden, and they smell like a barn on a hot day. Families climb on low ones and pose inside open jaws, there are food stalls and local rice, and the setting is relaxed and rural. It is a sculpture display rather than a parade, so the pieces stay on show for weeks into autumn and can be seen at your own pace.
experiences.wonderMoment: Rounding the lake to find a two-story straw dinosaur rearing up against Mount Kakuda, every strand catching the late-summer light.

experiences.story:
The Balloon Fiesta began in 1972 with 13 balloons in a shopping-mall parking lot; it is now a nine-day event with several hundred balloons from dozens of countries. Its heart is the mass ascension: in the early morning, waves of balloons inflate and launch from a 365-acre field, steered by the light morning winds of the Rio Grande valley known as the Albuquerque Box. Special-shape days bring balloons shaped like animals, cartoon characters and objects.

You arrive in the cold dark, with breakfast burritos and coffee. Before sunrise, a few "dawn patrol" balloons glow overhead, then the field fills with roaring burners and slowly rising fabric. You can walk right up to crews as envelopes swell beside you. By the time the sun clears the Sandias, the sky holds hundreds of balloons at once. Evening glows, when tethered balloons light up together after dark, are just as striking.
experiences.wonderMoment: Just after sunrise, when wave after wave lifts off and the whole sky over the Rio Grande fills with balloons.

experiences.location: Oaxaca de Juárez and surrounding villages, Oaxaca
experiences.dateDetails: Oct 31–Nov 2 every year (Nov 1 for children, Nov 2 for adults); cemetery vigils peak the nights of Oct 31 and Nov 1. Comparsas and markets build through late October; 2027 city program not yet announced.

experiences.tagline: Marigold paths, candlelit graves and brass-band skeletons dancing until dawn
experiences.story:
Day of the Dead blends pre-Hispanic rites for the dead with the Catholic feasts of All Saints and All Souls. In Oaxaca, families build ofrendas (home altars) loaded with marigolds, pan de muerto, mole, mezcal and photos of the dead, and lay paths of orange petals so the souls can find their way home. UNESCO listed Mexico's indigenous festivities for the dead in 2008.

At night the cemeteries fill. At Xoxocotlán and Atzompa, thousands of candles light the graves, copal smoke drifts between the tombs, and families sit through the night eating, talking and hiring musicians to play the dead person's favorite songs. In the city and the Etla valley, comparsas and muerteadas take over the streets: masked dancers dressed as skeletons, devils and catrinas follow brass bands, setting off firecrackers and pulling onlookers in to dance.
experiences.wonderMoment: Walking into the Xoxocotlán cemetery after midnight, when every grave glows with candles and a band plays softly for someone's grandmother.

On the first Sunday of October, human-powered sculptures run a course through town, onto the beach, into the bay and through a deep mud bog. The mood is wet and joyful. Fall light comes low over the water, the brick downtown is full of costumed teams, and there is a lot of cheering for whoever is most stuck. Spectators line the streets and the water entry, and the town is compact enough to see several stages. Downtown viewing is on pavement; the beach and mud sections are on uneven ground.

experiences.story:
Hanal Pixán means "food of the souls" in Yucatec Maya, and it is the Yucatán's version of Day of the Dead, from October 31 to November 2. Families build altars with marigolds, candles, photographs and mucbipollo, a large tamale baked underground. In Mérida, the city's Festival de las Ánimas centers on the Paseo de las Ánimas, a procession from the General Cemetery through the old neighborhoods to San Juan park.

The procession is quiet compared to Mexico City's parades. People with skull-painted faces walk in embroidered white huipiles, carrying candles; the street is lined with altars and the air smells of copal incense and wax. Parks fill with altar displays and food stands. The route is on city streets, which helps, though crowds are dense; watching from a fixed spot near the end is easiest.

experiences.tagline: A 14-metre mechanical Minotaur breathes smoke beside a Toulouse airfield
experiences.story:
La Machine is the Nantes-based street theatre company of François Delarozière, known for vast moving creatures made of wood, steel and leather: the Grand Éléphant in Nantes, the dragon-horse Long Ma, giant spiders. In Toulouse, the Halle de La Machine opened in 2018 on the old Montaudran airfield, home to Astérion the Minotaur and dozens of smaller machines you can watch in motion and sometimes ride.

In autumn the Halle hosts Mécanik Paradize, an electronic music night where DJs play among the machines as they move, light and smoke. Big street shows tour less often, but when they happen, a creature taller than a house walks through a city for days with musicians and acrobats aboard. experiences.story:
On November 1 the towns of Sumpango and Santiago Sacatepéquez in Guatemala's highlands display giant round kites made of tissue paper and bamboo. Teams spend months building them; the largest reach up to about 20 meters across and are raised as standing displays, while smaller ones are flown. The kites carry messages and images about Maya identity, history and the dead, and tradition holds that they carry messages to the spirits. The kite-making technique has national heritage status in Guatemala.

The scale and color hit you first: huge geometric mandalas of red, gold and turquoise paper, lifted upright with ropes by dozens of people. There is the smell of food, the snap of paper in the wind and cheers when a flying kite climbs, or falls. In Santiago the kites are in the cemetery among the graves. Sumpango's festival is on a large open field, which is easier to reach and to watch from a seat.

experiences.tagline: Devon locals sprint flaming tar barrels on their shoulders through packed streets
experiences.story:
On the night of 5 November, the small Devon town of Ottery St Mary keeps one of England's strangest Bonfire Night customs. Seventeen wooden barrels, lined with tar and set alight, are hoisted onto the shoulders of local people who run with them through the streets until the barrel is too hot or burnt out. Each pub hosts a barrel, and families have carried them for generations; only those born or long resident in the town may take part.

The crowd presses in close, so you feel the heat and smell tar smoke as the runner charges toward you. Spectators scatter, then pack back in. Women's and boys' barrels come earlier in the evening; the biggest, heaviest barrels come near midnight in the square. Nearby there is a big bonfire and a funfair, but the barrels are the reason thousands arrive.
experiences.wonderMoment: Near midnight the largest barrel is lit in the square and a runner in sacking gloves bursts through the crowd with a column of flame above his head.

experiences.story:
Pushkar is one of Hinduism's holiest towns, built around a lake said to have formed where Brahma dropped a lotus. Each autumn, in the days leading to the full moon of Kartik, herders from across Rajasthan walk their camels, horses and cattle to the dunes outside town to trade. Around the market grows a fair: camel races and dances, a moustache contest, and pilgrims arriving to bathe in the lake on the full moon.

At dawn the dunes are covered with camels lying in rows, smoke from dung fires drifting through low sun, and men in bright turbans haggling over animals. The camels wear pom-poms, bells and patterns clipped into their fur. Evenings bring folk singers, Kalbelia dancers and a Ferris wheel lit against the sky, while the ghats fill with lamps and the clang of temple bells.

experiences.tagline: Lamps on every step of Varanasi's riverfront on the Kartik full moon
experiences.story:
Dev Deepawali, the Diwali of the gods, falls fifteen days after Diwali, on the full moon of the month of Kartik. Tradition says the gods descend to bathe in the Ganges that night to celebrate Shiva's victory over the demon Tripurasura. Since the 1980s Varanasi has answered by lighting its ghats, the stone stairs that run for kilometres along the river, with clay oil lamps; recent years have counted lamps in the hundreds of thousands to over a million.

By late afternoon families and volunteers are setting diyas in lines on every step. At dusk they are lit one by one, and the whole curve of the riverbank turns gold and doubles in the water. Conch shells sound for the Ganga Aarti at Dashashwamedh Ghat, brass lamps swing in unison, marigolds and small leaf boats of flame drift downstream, and fireworks go up over the far bank. The river is jammed with rowing boats, the best place to see the whole arc at once.
experiences.wonderMoment: From a boat in midstream as the last lamps are lit, the entire crescent of ghats glows at once and its reflection fills the Ganges.

experiences.story:
Yi Peng is the northern Thai (Lanna) festival of the full moon of the second Lanna month, and it coincides with Loy Krathong, celebrated across Thailand on the full moon of the twelfth month. Together they make Chiang Mai's biggest week. Temples and lanes hang hundreds of paper lanterns, people float krathong (small rafts of banana leaf, flowers, incense and a candle) on the Ping River to let go of bad luck, and a parade of lit floats and dancers moves through the old city.

At night the old city smells of incense and candle wax. Monks chant at Wat Phan Tao under strings of orange lanterns; on the river bridges people crouch to launch their krathong while firecrackers pop overhead. Khom loi, the paper hot-air lanterns, drift up singly from riversides and in their thousands at organised releases outside the city, where a crowd lights wicks together and lets go on a signal.
experiences.wonderMoment: On a signal thousands of glowing paper lanterns lift off at once and drift up toward the full moon like a slow, silent river of light.

experiences.story:
Nuremberg's Christkindlesmarkt fills the Hauptmarkt below the Gothic Frauenkirche with about 180 red-and-white striped wooden stalls, the 'little town of wood and cloth' locals talk about. Its roots go back to the 1600s. The rules are strict: no plastic garlands or piped pop music, and traditional goods come first. That means Lebkuchen (spiced gingerbread), finger-sized Nuremberg sausages, gold-foil Rauschgoldengel (tinsel angels) and Zwetschgenmännle, little figures made of dried prunes.

The market opens on the Friday before Advent, when the Christkind (a local teenager elected every two years to play the Christmas angel) steps onto the Frauenkirche balcony in golden robes and a tall gold crown. Tens of thousands crowd the square in the cold and go quiet while she recites the prologue, a short rhymed speech written in the 20th century. When she finishes, the stall lights come on, the church bells ring, and the smell of mulled wine and roasting almonds rises over the crowd.
experiences.wonderMoment: The square falls silent as the Christkind, in gold on the Frauenkirche balcony, speaks the prologue, and then every stall lights up at once.

experiences.tagline: Horned, fur-covered demons with cowbells storm Alpine towns in the dark
experiences.story:
In early December, Salzburg and towns across Alpine Austria hold Krampus runs. The Krampus is St Nicholas's dark companion, a horned figure in goat or sheep fur with a hand-carved wooden mask, a switch of birch twigs and heavy bells strapped to his back. In the same season, Perchten groups parade figures that are meant to drive out winter spirits. Many masks are carved by local craftsmen and passed down.

The Krampuslauf is loud before it is visible: hundreds of bells clanging in a steady rhythm, then torchlight, smoke and the masks coming out of the dark. Krampuses lunge at the barriers, swat at legs with twigs, and growl at teenagers who dare them. Children cling to parents and laugh at once. Afterwards there is mulled wine and roasted chestnuts at the Christmas market, under baroque church towers and snow-dusted mountains.
experiences.wonderMoment: The street goes dark, the bells start somewhere you can't see, and a line of horned masks lit by torches walks out of the smoke toward you.

experiences.story:
Nagaland, in the far northeast of India on the border with Myanmar, is home to more than a dozen Naga tribes, each with its own language, dress and songs. Since 2000 the state has brought them together for ten days every December at Kisama Heritage Village, a few kilometres from Kohima. The festival is named for the great hornbill, a bird that appears in Naga folklore and whose feathers are worn in ceremonial headdresses.

Each tribe builds or keeps its own morung, a traditional house with carved posts, buffalo skulls and bamboo walls, set along the hillside. In the central arena, lines of men in red and black shawls, cowrie shells, boar tusks and feathered helmets stamp and shout through war dances, while women in striped wraps sing harvest songs. There is the smell of woodsmoke, smoked pork and rice beer in bamboo cups, plus wrestling, chili-eating contests and rock concerts in Kohima at night. Morning mist sits in the valleys below.
experiences.wonderMoment: A line of Naga warriors in hornbill-feather headdresses charges into the arena with spears raised, chanting in unison as the hills behind them come out of the mist.

experiences.story:
Noche de Rábanos has taken place in Oaxaca's central plaza every December 23 since 1897. Farmers grow special oversized radishes, some longer than an arm and twisted into odd shapes, and artisans carve them into nativity scenes, saints, musicians, dancers and whole village scenes. Smaller categories use dried flowers and corn husks. The work lasts only a few hours before the radishes wilt.

The zócalo is packed and festive in the cool December evening. People queue for hours to file past the displays, under strings of lights, with church bells, brass bands and vendors selling buñuelos and hot drinks. Up close the radish red-and-white is surprising: carved skin becomes robes, the white flesh becomes faces. Fireworks often end the night. Lines can be long and on foot, so going early in the afternoon is wise.
experiences.wonderMoment: When you reach the front of the line and see a whole Guelaguetza dance troupe carved from radishes, glistening under the lights.

experiences.story:
San Fernando in Pampanga calls itself the Christmas Capital of the Philippines because of its parol, star-shaped lanterns that Filipino families hang for the season. The Ligligan Parul, held each December, is a contest between the city's barangays (neighbourhoods), each building one giant lantern up to about six metres across, covered in thousands of light bulbs and colored plastic.

The art is in the motion. Behind each lantern, technicians run the lights using a barrel-like rotor, a drum of bent hairpins that switches bulbs on and off in sequence by hand. As the competition music plays, the lanterns bloom and spiral in colour, petals opening, stars spinning, patterns rippling outward. The crowd, warm in the tropical December night, cheers for their barangay. The festival grew out of the lantern processions of the Lubenas, held before Christmas in the area, and the craft of building lanterns is passed down in local families.
experiences.wonderMoment: When the music starts and a whole giant lantern bursts into rippling, spinning colour, petals of light chasing each other in time to the beat.
